text: Dana sat in the car outside the hospice for almost forty minutes before she turned the key. Her father had asked for the radio to stay off, so the car was silent except for the tick of the cooling engine. Inside, the nurse had already folded his reading glasses into their case and set them on the windowsill, beside a cup of melted ice nobody had thrown away. Dana had expected the sorrow to arrive all at once, like a dropped plate. Instead it came in small, ordinary pieces: the parking ticket she had forgotten to pay, the voicemail from the insurance company, the pharmacy receipt still folded in her coat pocket. She thought about calling her brother in Denver, then decided he would only ask whether the morphine had been adjusted, and she could not bear another question with a clinical answer. The grief had no shape yet. It was only the weight of a coat she could not take off. When she finally walked back through the sliding doors, the receptionist looked up with the careful face people wear for strangers who have just lost someone, and Dana understood that this was now how the world would see her. She was sad in a way that had no edges, and she had to drive home anyway.

Title: My dad's dog died last night and I can't stop thinking about it at work

I'm 34, I live two states away from my parents, and I was the one who talked my dad into adopting Biscuit after Mom passed. He's 71 and said he didn't do well alone, so the dog was supposed to be company. Last night the vet called at 9:40 to say his kidneys had failed and they could not save him. Dad was alone in the kitchen when they told him. He called me afterward and just said, "He's gone, kiddo," and then nothing for a long time.

I'm writing this because I feel so sad and guilty. I should have flown out in October when he first got sick. I told myself it was minor. Now every room in my apartment feels wrong, and I keep hearing the jingle of his tags in the hallway that isn't there.

My boss noticed I'd been staring at the same spreadsheet all morning and asked if I was okay, and I just nodded because I didn't want to explain. Has anyone dealt with grief over a pet while also worrying about a parent living alone? How did you get through the first week? I don't know what I'm asking for, honestly. I just needed to put it somewhere.

Hi Marcus,

I hope the new job is treating you better than the last one did. I wanted to tell you something before I lose my nerve, and I'd rather you hear it from me than from Jen. Sam and I are separating. We told the kids on Sunday, which was the worst afternoon of my life so far. Maya asked whether we were still a family, and I didn't have an answer that wasn't a lie.

I know you'll say I should see a counselor, and I do, twice a month. Honestly the sadness comes in waves. Some mornings I'm fine making coffee, and then I see his mug still in the drying rack and I'm sitting on the kitchen floor. Some of it is grief for a marriage I thought would last my whole life.

Work has been a bit of a shelter, but I've been making mistakes on the quarterly reports, and Priya covered for me twice without saying anything, which somehow made it worse. I feel ashamed and exhausted and a bit numb.

I'm not asking you to fix anything. I just didn't want to disappear on you. Can we get a beer when you're back in town? I'd like to see a face that remembers what we were like before all this.

Love,
Rachel

Mom's bank statements arrived in a manila envelope with her handwriting on the front. I put them on the counter and made pasta I didn't eat. Sorted her pill organizer into the bin for the pharmacy, Thursday's compartment still full, which means she skipped it again, or forgot, or did not see the point. Called the funeral home back to confirm the flowers. The woman on the phone asked if I wanted the lilies or the white roses, and I said whatever was cheapest, then felt I'd said something unforgivable. Drove past the house on the way home. The porch light was off. Someone had already taken the wind chime down. Ate standing up. Put her cardigan in the washer by mistake and had to fish it out before it hit the spin. Her reading glasses are still on the arm of the chair. I have not moved them. Set two alarms for tomorrow because I keep waking at five and lying there listening to the refrigerator. Work sent the agenda for Thursday's meeting. I opened it, read the first line, closed it.

Ray had been driving to the cemetery every Sunday since March, which he told his son was for the exercise. The stone was still a blank slab of gray granite with Helen's name cut in and nothing else yet. He brought a folding chair, a thermos, and the crossword from the paper, though he rarely finished it. Other people's graves had flowers, plastic windmills, a child's painted rock. His wife's stayed bare. The groundskeeper, a young man with a sunburned neck, nodded at him from the mower and said the sod was taking nicely. At home the spare bedroom still held her sewing machine under its quilted cover, and the fridge still had her yogurt, past its date, which he could not bring himself to throw out. He had started eating dinner at the counter so he would not have to look at the empty chair. The phone rang on Thursdays. It was usually the church, asking whether he would bring a casserole to the Tuesday group. He always said yes, then forgot, then felt the forgetting like a stone in his shoe.
